events: Birth in London (13 July 1527): John Dee was born in London into a family whose Welsh connections and later claims of British antiquity would matter to his self-fashioning.
Studies at St John's College, Cambridge (1542): Dee entered Cambridge as a young scholar and was trained in the logical, mathematical, and humanist disciplines that underwrote his later reputation.
Becomes a founding fellow of Trinity College (1546): Dee became associated with the newly founded Trinity College and taught logic and sophistry in a university culture dependent on patronage.

Studies and networks at Louvain (1548-1550): At Louvain Dee entered a major center of mathematical, astronomical, and instrument culture, encountering figures and methods that shaped his technical authority.
Lectures on Euclid in Paris (1550): Dee's Paris lectures on Euclid helped establish his continental reputation as a mathematical teacher and interpreter.
Arrested under Mary I after astrological suspicion (1555): Dee's astrological and prognosticating expertise drew suspicion during Mary's reign, leading to imprisonment and examination.

Consulted around Elizabeth I's accession (1558-1559): Dee's astrological expertise became useful at the accession of Elizabeth I, including the broader culture of choosing auspicious times and reading royal futures.
Publishes Propaedeumata aphoristica (1558): Dee's Propaedeumata aphoristica presented aphorisms on celestial influence, rays, and natural causation.
Publishes Monas hieroglyphica (1564): Dee published the Monas hieroglyphica, a dense symbolic work joining mathematics, alchemy, cabala, and hieroglyphic interpretation.
Builds the Mortlake library (1560s-1570s): Dee developed the Mortlake library into a working scholarly collection used for reading, consultation, writing, and social exchange.
Writes the Mathematical Preface to Euclid (1570): Dee's preface to Billingsley's English Euclid defended mathematics as a practical and metaphysical discipline mediating visible and invisible orders.
Composes Brytannicae Reipublicae Synopsis (1570): Dee's Synopsis organized the Elizabethan commonwealth as a field for learned counsel and reform.
Publishes General and Rare Memorials (1576-1577): Dee's General and Rare Memorials advanced a program of navigation, maritime policy, and British imperial recovery.
Calendar reform counsel (1582): Dee participated in debates over calendar reform, where mathematical correction was inseparable from confessional and political caution.

First surviving angelic action (22 December 1581): The first surviving spirit action began Dee's extant record of angelic conversations, framed by prayer, discernment, and the search for divine wisdom.
Edward Kelley enters the angelic work (March 1582): Edward Kelley, initially known as Talbot, became Dee's principal scryer and the indispensable mediator of many later visions.
Heptarchical system takes shape (1582-1583): The angelic actions generated the ritual and angelic materials that Dee later organized as De Heptarchia Mystica.
Leaves England with Albert Laski (September 1583): Dee, his household, and Kelley left England with the Polish noble Albert Laski, carrying the angelic project into Central Europe.
Prague, Rudolf II, and imperial audiences (1584-1586): In Prague Dee sought audiences and recognition in a courtly world fascinated by alchemy, prophecy, and occult philosophy.
Revealed language, tables, and calls (1584): The angelic project produced revealed language, tables, calls, and names associated with later Enochian materials.
Třeboň years under Vilem Rozmberk (1586-1589): Dee and Kelley continued their angelic and alchemical work in Bohemia under elite patronage, while their partnership became increasingly strained.
The communion of wives crisis (April 1587): The angelic records reached a crisis in the command involving Dee and Kelley's wives, one of the most controversial episodes in the corpus.
Returns to England without Kelley (1589): Dee returned to England after the continental project fractured and Kelley pursued independent alchemical patronage.
Mortlake library damaged and dispersed (Late 1580s-1590s): During Dee's absence and later decline, the Mortlake library suffered loss, damage, and dispersal.
Appointed Warden of Manchester College (1595): Dee received the wardenship of Manchester College, an office that offered employment but placed him away from the courtly center he had long pursued.
Publishes the Apologetical Letter (1599): Dee's Apologetical Letter defended his reputation, listed his writings, and appealed against slanders of conjuring and unlawful magic.
Late angelic actions (1607): A small set of late actions shows Dee returning to angelic communication near the end of his life.
Death at Mortlake (1608 or 1609): Dee died in poverty and diminished public standing, though his books, manuscripts, objects, and reputation continued to circulate.
Casaubon publishes A True & Faithful Relation (1659): Meric Casaubon published Dee's angel diaries within a cautionary frame about spirits, delusion, and unlawful curiosity.
